en: [017.jpg-lower] = *Mahāmāyāpañjikā* of *Śrībhūṣaṇa*, from near the beginning: ...
the consecrations, the accomplishments, and the Vajra-Ḍākinīs.

Those known as Rin-me and Di-pa have accomplished the Ḍākinī; for that very reason, those who have accomplished Vajraḍākinī, whose nature is supreme primordial wisdom, abide in the sky because they are themselves unobservable.
The threefold [division of] body, speech, and mind is designated as "the secret.
(Samājottara 24ab)
By the term "secret" (*guhya*), the three—body, speech, and mind—are expressed;
they are secret because they are to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedya*) and are not the domain of others.
They are secret because, by virtue of being known directly by oneself, they are not the sphere of experience for others, like the sky.
Because he is endowed with the perfection of the welfare of both self and others, he is the Sovereign (*aiśvarya*). As it is taught in the *Samāja-tantra*, there are one hundred supreme families.
The threefold body, speech, and mind is designated as the "secret.
(Samājottara 37d) [and] (Samājottara 24ab).
Note: As stated in the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*:
"The five, the hundred families, and the three are declared to be the secrets of body, speech, and mind.

Therefore, the Blessed One Vajraḍāka, who consists of the hundred families of body, speech, and mind, is the teacher here. The compiler, however, is Buddhaḍākinī, who is also known by the name Mahāmāyā. As she will say: "O Goddess, I speak the truth," and so forth.
Because of that very [nature], the hundred families consist of the essence of body, speech, and mind.

The Blessed One Vajraḍākinī is the teacher here, while the Buddha-Ḍākinī, who possesses the name Mahāmāyā, is the compiler. As it has been said: "The five goddesses have spoken the truth," and so forth.

That very Blessed One is the subject to be expressed here. Furthermore, the sequence of realizations (*abhisamayānupūrvi*) for the sake of attaining him is also denoted by that term, as is the composition of words that explains him. That which is obtained is the most secret [reality]; that alone is called a *tantra*. It is so called because the Blessed One, or the sequence of realizations which is the cause for attaining the Blessed One, is woven (*tantryate*) or explained by means of it. The word "named" (*nāma*) signifies what is well-known.

For this very reason, the Blessed One speaks here; and because it is to be attained, the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is also expressed by that term, as it is applied to that which brings about such realization. Thus one finds [the passage]: "The great assembly of sounds, the sublime secret. For this very reason, it is called a *tantra* (*rgyud*), as the Blessed One has extensively explained.
As for the phrase "having gone forth," the expression "the Blessed One has composed this sequence of clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) as the cause for attainment" is a term signifying completion.

Desiring to investigate the secret, he said: “*Yayā*,” and so forth. By that (*yayā*) which has the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, the worlds of sentient beings and their environments are pervaded and consist of it; for according to the principle: “Since no phenomenon exists apart from the *dharmadhātu*,” or as it is said: “Emptiness is not other than phenomena, nor do phenomena exist without it. (Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra 13.11ab)
In the *Commentary on the Secret [Meaning]* (*Guhyavyākhyā*), it is stated:

Regarding the phrase "by which" (*yena*) and so forth, "by which" means by way of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. "Pervades" (*vyāpta*) means that its very essence is such, because there is no sentient world or container-world (*bhājanaloka*) that does not exist as inseparable from the *dharmadhātu*.
"By the cognition of 'no' (neti), emptiness is neither other than nor distinct from entities, nor do entities exist.
Oh dear, what a laugh! *tāṃ vinā iti vā* = "or [the phrase] 'without that'?
He also states its causality in the passage beginning with "*utpattiḥ*" (arising) and so forth. From that [emptiness], there is the arising of the four goddesses, Vajraḍākinī and the others.
Furthermore, its own cause shall also be explained: it is generated by those four goddesses, Vajraḍākinī and the others.
Regarding the term *brahman*, it refers to Vajraḍāka, whose nature is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the Buddhaḍākinīs and the others are also included.
"Brahmā" refers to Vajraḍākinī, who is the essence of non-dual gnosis; "and so forth" refers to the Buddhaḍākinīs and the rest.

Because great supernatural power (*mahatī ṛddhiḥ*), which is the perfection of the welfare of oneself and others, arises from this, they are called "possessors of great supernatural power" (*maharddhikāḥ*). To the question, "What is that supreme secret? he says: "This [is] of those Vajra-Ḍākinīs. He refers to what is present in the intellect as *Mahāmāyā*, whose form consists of white, subtle drops.

"Great Power" (*mthu chen*) refers to the great accomplishments and miraculous powers that are the attainments of both oneself and others. What is that? It is expressed by the phrase "their sublime secret," which refers to the Vajra Ḍākinīs. "This" refers to meditating while having placed it in the mind. "Great Illusion" (*sgyu ma chen po*) refers to the subtle, white form of the *bindu*.

She is called *Maheśvarī* because she is the cause of great sovereignty (*maheśvarya*). She is called *Mahāmāyā* because, like a great magical illusion (*mahendrajāla*), she consists of the manifestation of various forms while being empty of intrinsic reality. Regarding the term *Maheśvarī*, it is so called because she is the cause of great sovereignty. Regarding the term *Mahāmāyā*, it is so called because she is an illusion consisting of the appearance of diverse aspects within emptiness, just like the phenomena of a great optical illusion. [The four Māras...]

"She who is called the Great Dragmo" is so named because she subdues the four māras. "She who gathers the bhūtas" is so named because she performs emanation and reabsorption. "Pervasive" means that she acts for the benefit of sentient beings simultaneously in all directions. Regarding this very point, it is said in the *Vikurvaṇa-vistara*: "The Buddha is described as pervasive. Thus it is said. The world...
The so-called "three supports" (*rten gsum*) refers precisely to the desire, form, and formless realms; these themselves are what are to be clarified as the "caused" and the "uncaused."
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, going for refuge to the Three Jewels, generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*),
and taking up [the vows].

The accomplishment of the great commitment (*mahāsamayasiddhi*). The accomplishment that is not to be valued even by a great tantra is the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrāsiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "by means of the applications of Mahāmāyā": it refers to the meditations on drops (*bindu*) and seeds (*bīja*) which are like illusions. Regarding the phrase "the yoga-restraint" (*yogasamvara*): one should effect the supreme bliss of passion, which consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*). And that yoga-restraint is to be understood from the oral instructions of the Guru. By this, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is indicated.

"Accomplishment of the Great Samaya" refers to the great siddhi of priceless value, namely the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. "By means of the supreme application of the Great Illusion" refers to the meditations on the illusory-like *bindu* and seed-syllables. "The vow of yoga" refers to that which has the nature of method and wisdom.

This refers to being devoted to the supreme bliss of *candālī*. Furthermore, regarding this, the *Guru-upadeśa-yogasaṃvara* states: "By means of this called 'the essence of primordial wisdom' (*jñānātman*), one pursues the empowerments.

The "five offerings" (*pañcopahāra*) refer to the sacrificial cakes (*naivedya*) and so forth. The "five qualities of desire" (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) refer to the sublime [objects] such as form, sound, smell, and so on.

The supreme practitioner must understand this through reasoning and scripture from the true guru: by means of that aforementioned knowledge, when perfected through the power of meditative cultivation, one attains the accomplishment (*siddhi*) whose nature is non-abiding nirvāṇa—utterly transcending the two extremes characterized by the conceptualization of existence, non-existence, and so forth, and free from the two extremes; it is eternal due to its continuous flow, and its form is a drop (*bindu*) encircled by seven and a half qualities.

Regarding the phrase "by the lord of practitioners" (*sgrub po'i dbang pos*) and so forth, it is to be understood through the authority of the sublime gurus, as well as through reasoning and scripture. Regarding the phrase "by which gnosis" (*gang gis ye shes*), it refers to that which was just spoken by me. Regarding the phrase "by accomplishment" (*grub pas*), it means appearing as if manifest through the power of meditation. Regarding the word "thoroughly" (*shin tu*), it refers to [the realization of] existence, non-existence, and so forth.

It is the characteristic of meditation that suppresses the two extremes of existence and non-existence. What is called "attainment" (*siddhi*) is free from mental focal points; its nature is non-abiding nirvāṇa.
What is called "permanently" means that it is attained through continuous cultivation.

Having stabilized the mind through the application of the *bindu* and so forth by means of the series of syllables beginning with *a*, one becomes capable in every respect; thus he says, "showing," and so on. "Various kinds" refers to those various emanations (*nirmāṇa*). He explains exactly what the task is to be performed by means of these emanations: "attainment" (*siddhi*), meaning the eight great attainments and so forth; "the desired welfare of sentient beings"; and "the glory of the Tathāgatas," which is Buddhahood.

Either by means of the sequence beginning with the generation of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), or by way of the method of possession (*āveśana*), or by means of elixirs (*rasāyana*), that is, perfected substances.

By means of the phrases beginning with "With a garland of excellent syllables" (*yige dam pa'i phreng ba yis*) and so forth, it refers to the form of a *bindu* (drop) encircled by the transition of eight [syllables]. It is stated that if the mind is stabilized through the *bindu-yoga* and other such practices, one will become capable in every respect. Regarding the phrase "it will be seen" (*mthong bar 'gyur*) and so forth, it refers to whatever various forms of emanations (*nirmāṇa*) are emanated.

"Having performed [the ritual], he speaks. Regarding the phrase "by the Tathāgata," it means that Buddhahood is accomplished through the sequence of generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) or the sequence of descending [into the womb]. "Siddhi" refers to the benefit of sentient beings, which is the aspiration for the eight great siddhis and so forth. "Rasāyana" refers to the substances of accomplishment.

He states the summary of the expansion of the ritual activities (*karmaprasara*), beginning with "In semen" (*śukre*) and so forth. In the drawing-in of the *piṇḍa*, the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) comes through the atmosphere; in the drawing-in by foot, [he comes] on foot. "Seven births," etc., refers to human flesh. He describes the power of those who have attained the lower accomplishments (*hīnasiddhi*): "Great longevity" means lasting for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). "Miraculous power" (*prātihārya*) consists of blazing, heating, and so forth. "A body that cannot be satiated" means a sight that never causes weariness. "Transformation of form" means taking the form of a tiger and so forth. "By mere thought" means by the simple act of wishing.

Regarding the statement "The Extensive Exposition in Brief," it begins with the words "semen" (*khuba*) and so forth. What was previously referred to as "summoning" (*dgug pa*) refers to the light that appears as the object to be accomplished. When the garland of seven births and so forth, as well as the flesh of those who have been born, are summoned, the majesty of accomplishment is described; "longevity" (*tshe ring*) means abiding for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). And [there is] the body of the wrathful one.

"Yang" means to cause displeasure upon seeing [something]. "Miracle" (*cho 'phrul*) refers to such things as blazing and burning. "Intention" (*bsam pa*) means by mere desire. "Form is completely transformed" (*gzugs ni yongs su bsgyur*) means into the forms of tigers and so forth. He speaks of the greatness of the *tantra*: "The sovereign of the sciences (*vidyā*), the principal one... [vi-019.jpg-lower]... gone.

Mahāmāyā is perfected through recitation for one who is free from defilement; she is unfailing and fruitful. Vajraḍāka says: "In my opinion, there is no other vidyā equal to her, among all the worlds and within all the tantras, such as the Saṃvara and others."

"Great Vidyā" (Rig ma chen mo) is the name; she is the exceedingly great self. "Mistress" (Dbang phyug) means the sovereign lady. "Great Illusion" (Sgyu ma che) means she is free from sin. "Accomplished through recitation, the Unbewildered One" means she possesses the fruit [of practice]. By this, it is meant that there is no vidyā equal to her. When he says "I," it refers to the Vajraḍākinī, the mistress of all worlds throughout the migrations.
"This is the scripture; this is the scripture," thus it was said to you by the Buddha-Ḍākinī. "O beautiful one! O you who are delightful in every aspect!
Regarding the phrase "these scriptures are known" and "it has been explained to you," this refers to the Buddha’s [explanation] to the Ḍākinī.

The accomplishments of the Great Vidyā and the accomplishment of the state of a Vajradhara belonging to the Yogīśvarī just mentioned are manifested as those five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and so forth. Those are now being pointed out; the text by which they are described is referred to in that manner.

Immediately thereafter, he spoke: "The Vajra-siddhi of the Great Siddha-Vidyādhara Lord of Yogins. "Signs" refers to the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and so forth. "That which is taught by them" refers to whichever *dhāraṇī* was spoken in such a manner.
In the first [chapter], there is a dependence on the second. || 0 ||
"First" (*prathama*) is in relation to a "second. *Atheti* means immediately after the initial designation.
"Then" (*tataḥ*) refers to that which follows right after what was first taught.

It is "Divine" (*divya*) because it is free from existence such as *nirvāṇa* and the like; it is "Secret" (*guhya*) because its nature consists of body, speech, and mind; it is "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) because it does not decay within the *dharmadhātu*; it is that which is to be recited, beginning with the syllable *Oṃ*. Regarding the term "Secret": it is so called because its essence is body, speech, and mind. Regarding the term "Syllable" (*yi ge*, *akṣara*): it refers to the recitation of *Oṃ* and so forth, because it does not change within the *dharmadhātu*. Regarding the term "Sublime" (*dam pa*, *parama*): it refers to *nirvāṇa* and the like, because it is free from worldly existence (*bhava*).

Yoga-siddhi is the accomplishment of the nature of the self, which consists of the uncontaminated bliss of method and wisdom. As it has been said: "The union of wisdom and method is designated as yoga. That which is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is wisdom; [the other] is method, characterized by existence. This is the fruit, because of the successful establishment of the welfare of oneself and others.
Because it is renowned for accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others,
it bestows that [attainment].

Regarding that which was spoken as suchness: "The union of method and wisdom is explicitly designated as 'yoga. That which, by way of method and wisdom, is devoid of characteristics and intrinsic nature—this is what is meant. Furthermore, that very state is called "the fruit," because it is the excellence of the accomplishments for the benefit of oneself and others. Regarding the statement that his mind is exalted, it begins with the words "by which," and so forth.

Thinking that even such reflection is for the sake of the highest good (*śreyas*), he says: "By which," and so forth. It would be better if there were eight [syllables]... [omitted] ...which bestows the siddhis of the Buddha’s methods and so forth. Another is the syllable *Oṃ*. At the time of recitation, it is the radiating [emanation]; because it has the nature of teaching, its intrinsic nature is the *nirmāṇakāya*. The firm establishment of the abode of the syllables of the body is the splendor of the *dharmakāya*. The *Hūṃ* is the essence of the *cittavajra*. "Supreme" (*mchog*) means that which is intensely desired; it is that which bestows those [attainments], such as the eight siddhis of the Buddhas.

The so-called "first syllable" is *Oṃ*, which is the emanation at the time of recitation. Because it functions as the mode of manifestation, it is the nature of the *nirmāṇakāya*. *Oṃ* is the syllable of the body and possesses the identity of the *saṃbhogakāya*. *Hūṃ* possesses the identity of the *cittavajra* (mind-vajra) and is taught as the actual object of abiding.
Furthermore, *Oṃ* is to be recited by pervading the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and effort (*āyāma*).

One should recite while engaged in breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). The meaning of the phrase "the yogi performs exhalation" (*ucchvāsaṃ kurute*) is as follows: the letter *ha*, which is the end of the eight—that is, the end of the group of eight vowels—is joined below with the vowel *ū*. "With a bindu" means having the crescent moon (*ardhendu*) as its head. The meaning is that one should perform the recitation (*jāpa*) free from the conceptualization of existence and non-existence. "Its uttered speech is not proclaimed" means that in the stream of nectar (*amṛtadhārā*), the distinction between self and other, and the higher and lower, ceases and subsides.

"The phrase 'the *dbugs* (breaths) are to be emitted' refers to the purpose of this yogin. 'The end of the eight' means the end of the eight great classes (*sde chen*), which is the form of the letter *ha*. 'The one joined with *au*' means it is provided with [the vowel] below. 'Together with the bindu' means the half-moon at the crown of the head. 'Entity and non-entity' means that the recitation should be performed free from mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Regarding that:

Regarding the statement "there is no explanation of the *bhr̥kuṭī*," it means that by means of the flow of nectar (*amr̥ta*), one becomes free from the distinction between self and other; thus, one turns back from this state to that, and becomes the master of asceticism (*tapas*).

He states the meaning of the yoga just mentioned: "Mantra" refers to the syllable *hūṃ* and so forth; "form" (*saṃsthāna*) refers to the appearance of the deity; "phenomenon" (*dharma*) refers to the *dharmadhātu*.
Immediately following that, the *Yogārthabhāṣya* states: "Mantra" refers to *hūṃ* and so forth; "form" (*mūrti*) refers to the aspect of the deity; and "dharma" refers to the *dharmadhātu*.
Mahāmāyāpañjikā X, recto.

Some say that in the maṇḍala there is an eight-petalled [lotus]; therein, upon a solar disc, are five white drops. It is joined by four goddesses produced from the drops in the four directions. Afterwards, following the exhortation by means of that song, there arises from the central drop a Vajraḍāka born from the syllable *hūṃ*.

Some say it is a four-petaled red lotus; others say it is eight-petaled. In the visualization mandala, it has four petals, while in the four painted mandalas, it has eight petals. Therein, upon the solar mandala, are five white *bindus*. It is endowed with the four goddesses arising from the moon in the four directions, and immediately thereafter, they exhort him with song.
In the center, from a drop (*bindu*) arisen from the syllable *Hūṃ*, there is the Vajradākinī born from that *Hūṃ*.

[The text says: "adorned with the forms of the Buddhas. He states the colors of the four faces of the Blessed One with the words beginning "in the east," and so forth. The goddesses also have four faces; their primary faces are yellow and so on. In their places, blue should be seen where yellow and the other colors were previously mentioned.

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha’s image is beautiful," this refers to the Bhagavān with four faces. As for the description of his body color, the words "to the east" and so forth indicate that the goddesses also have four faces and yellow body colors, and so on. In these cases, where the primary face is yellow and so forth, one should visualize it as blue in that particular position.

"All [deities] have four arms and three eyes. He now states the symbols (*cihna*) of the goddesses, beginning with "In the left," and so forth. To clarify that the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) is to be meditated upon immediately after the completion of the goddesses, he says "In the body" (*kāye*). The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "afterwards. "In the middle" means among the goddesses. "Therein" means upon the red lotus. He states the symbols of the Blessed One, beginning with "The skull," and so forth. This is what is meant:

Following the completion of the goddesses, there is the completion of the Blessed One. This refutes the opinion of those who claim that the completion of the goddesses occurs at the very same time as the completion of the Blessed One. [The four goddesses...]

Since, in this text, the reading of the four goddesses occurs at the very beginning and that of the Blessed One follows later—and since the description of the weapons of the goddesses is stated first and that of the Blessed One later—it is evident that the Blessed One’s manifestation occurs after the exhortation by the goddesses; nor is it appropriate for this [text] to follow the sequence of other tantras.

[He has] four arms and three eyes. Regarding the statement of the goddesses' characteristics, "on the left," and so forth: immediately after generating the goddesses, the Blessed One is generated. As for those who claim that the goddesses are generated at the very same time as the Blessed One is generated, I shall refute their position. Why? Because [there are] the four goddesses and...

Regarding the passage, "Possessing equanimity, the image of the Buddha is resplendent," this text first mentions the four goddesses and subsequently the Blessed One (*bhagavān*). Since the Blessed One is mentioned later as the one who is indicated by the symbols of the goddesses and so forth, as well as by the directions and so forth, the Blessed One’s generation occurs immediately after the goddesses have exhorted him with song;
it is not the same as in other tantras.

Since this [deity] is indeed distinct; furthermore, it is observed even in such tantras as the *Mārīcī-tantra* and others that, following the impulsion of light rays from the other goddesses who act as attendants (*upanāyikā*), the Blessed Lady who resides in the center is manifested.

Regarding the statement of the *Ḍākinī-mūla-tantra*: "For this very reason, those who are distinct [from one another] should be viewed as belonging to the *Prabhāvatī* and other tantras; it is said that the goddesses, being exhorted by the light rays generated by the principal suns, subsequently cause the Blessed Lord, the principal [deity], to abide in the center and generate [the retinue].

"With the initial mantra" means with the six syllables beginning with *oṃ*. One should visualize them joined with the six locations. "Blazing" means that one becomes the one who radiates and reabsorbs [light].

Regarding the phrase "the first mantra," it refers to *Oṃ*; one should meditate on being joined with the six syllables at the six locations. Regarding the word "intermediate," it refers to the process of emanation and reabsorption.
Thus, a yogin who possesses such union with the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) becomes capable of all accomplishments (*sādhana*). So it is said: "In this way" (*evam*).
Thus, the yogin who has become such through the yoga of the deity is empowered for all attainments.
It is said, "it becomes manifest" (*par'gyur ro*);

*dravya* refers to pills and so forth. Accomplishment (*siddhi*) is the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). Its fruit is the welfare of others. It is the display of all magical emanations. Its bestower—[continues with 013.jpg-lower] = 10\recto.
"In this way" refers to substances such as pills and the like. "Accomplished" refers to the siddhi of Mahāmāyā. Its fruit is the benefit of others, which is the manifestation of all illusions.
*Mahāmāyāpañjikā of Vibhūṣita* [Tōh. 1625]
Perhaps more likely *Śrībhūṣaṇa;
he is also the author of the *Daśatattva,
though otherwise his original works remain unknown.

—[this] is established in [the state of] *vati*. That is not [it]. He speaks of the benefits for those who have attained inferior success (*hīnasiddhi*). "Within" (*antar*) refers to the purification of nectar (*amṛtaśodhana*). "Of the reversed ones" refers to the conjunction of the three syllables. "Therein" means: one should visualize the substance empowered by the syllable *HŪṂ* as a pill joined with liquor and vajra-water within a skull-cup produced from the syllable *ĀḤ*, and subsequently visualize the syllable *OṂ*.

"Bestowing the gift" (*de rab sbyin*) means for the sake of accomplishing that. The mantra for accomplishing the non-inferior siddhi is spoken. "Invisible" (*mi snang ba*) means it is spoken so as to be unseen. "Reversal" (*bzlog pa*) refers to the yoga of the three syllables. "Therein" (*de la*) refers to the pill (*ril bu*) which is perfectly endowed with vajra water and consecrated by *hūṃ*.
One should place it upon a skull born from a corpse and meditate on the syllable *Oṃ* on its exterior.

He states the extraction of the mantra for the purpose of consecration (*abhimantraṇa*): **aṣṭe** is the final syllable. **sarve** refers to the yoga of the wheel of the four goddesses. The first syllable is *oṃ*; the syllable *āḥ* is not mentioned here. To explain its significance, he says **trīṇi**, etc. The meaning is that when the syllable *āḥ* is inserted in the middle, there become three.

Regarding the statement that "the mantra was extracted for the purpose of the *abhiṣṭuta* (highly praised)": the word "eight" (*aṣṭa*) is the final syllable. The word "all" (*sarva*) is the first syllable, *oṃ*, [derived] from the yoga of the four goddesses as world-rulers (*cakravartin*). The syllable *āḥ* is not mentioned here.
To explain its meaning, the phrase beginning with "three" (*tri*) and so forth indicates that *āḥ* is inserted into the center; thus, it means "it becomes three."

By this, the following is meant: having meditated upon the substance contained within a skull-cup and lotus vessel produced from the syllable *A*—resting upon the circles of wind and fire (and space)—together with the syllable *HŪṂ*; and having burned away impurities by means of the flames from the fire-circle ignited by the wind-circle below; and having rendered it of the nature of the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*); and having brought down the assembly of Victors (*jinavṛnda*) above by means of the rays of light from the syllable *OṂ*, and having made them of one taste (*samarasīkṛtya*); and having consecrated it with the mantra: *OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ GUHYĪ BHAKṢĀ BHAKṢE 'HAM*; one should draw it in through the tube of the vajra-gullet of the tongue and partake of it.
Having consecrated [the substances] with the mantra, it was said:

"Upon the wind mandala and so forth, one visualizes the substances placed within a lotus vessel born from the syllable ĀḤ, together with the syllable HŪṂ. Then, by means of the wind mandala from below and the blazing [fire], the sins are incinerated."

Having transformed [the food] into the nature of the nectar of primordial wisdom (*jñānāmṛta*), one should invite the assembly of Victors above with light rays from the *Oṃ* syllable and bring them to a state of equal flavor. Then, having performed the recitation: *Oṃ āḥ guhya bhāsha saṃbhāshaya hūṃ*, one should consume [the food] by drawing it in with the light rays from the tip of the vajra-linga of the tongue.

Explaining [the practice] for one endowed with the yoga-vow (*yogasamvara*), he says: “*Aṣṭa*,” and so forth. By this, there is the secret vajra produced from the syllable *hūṃ*. “By the union with the first syllable” means the jewel produced from the syllable *oṃ*. “By the syllable *hrīḥ*” means the lotus of the goddess produced from the syllable *hrīḥ*. “Having joined it with the final syllable” means the vajra-pore interspersed with the syllable *phaṭ*. “Employing the five seed-syllables” refers to the woman who possesses the five families (*pañcakula*).

"One should visualize by means of the syllable" refers to the yellow pericarp fashioned from the syllable *bhrūṃ*. "Having thus attained union" means having performed the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Regarding the statement "the eight," and so forth, this refers to the secret vajra emanated from the syllable *hūṃ*. "By means of the conjunction with the first syllable" refers to the jewel emanated from *oṃ*. "And *hrīḥ*" refers to *hrīḥ*.

"Having joined the syllable at the end" means that the *vajra* seed-syllable *phaṭ* is inserted within. "The five seed-syllables are thoroughly joined" means that they possess the portions of the five families. "The syllables are to be visualized" refers to the yellow syllable *brūm* arising from the center.
"This application should be understood" means that one should enter into meditative union (*samāpatti*).

When there is the dance of the Vajraḍākinīs accompanied by this song, one should establish Vajrasattva in the state of Heruka; one should meditate upon him in the center of the maṇḍala. "Yoga" is defined as the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). The accomplishment of yoga is the accomplishment whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means.
(From the *Samājottara*)

By this very vajra dance, that which is called "Vajrasattva" is Heruka; "to be introduced" means one should meditate in the manner of the vajra gaze. "Yoga is explicitly expressed as the union of method and wisdom. Regarding "yoga-siddhi," it is the siddhi whose nature consists of method and wisdom.

Through the practice of the four junctions (*catuḥsandhyā*) and supreme meditations, by practicing with reverence, continuously, and for a long time, one attains the supreme [state]. Adorned with the five objects of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) and embellished with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one obtains the accomplishment (*siddhi*) mentioned immediately above. To the question "What would happen through that?", he says: "Just like the bestower of the three bodies (*trikāya*). This means that as a bestower of boons (*varada*), consisting of the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-body, he becomes just like a perfectly awakened Buddha (*saṃbuddha*), granting the desired aims of all sentient beings.

Regarding "the supreme meditation through application during the four sessions," this means that by making it excellent, being continuously endowed with it for a long duration constitutes the supreme meditation. Regarding "filled with the qualities of desire," this refers to being adorned with the five offerings; as it is said, one attains the siddhi of the [deity's] form. If one asks what happens then: **thus, the supreme bestower of the three bodies.**

Thus it was said: "The supreme bestower, whose nature consists of the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya, grants the desired objects to all sentient beings; that is to say, he becomes here another perfect Buddha. *nirmāṇakāyātmake* = 11\recto.

He describes the power of the perfected one (*siddha*) with the words beginning "In a *yojana*," and so forth. He states that immediately after the meditation on union, one should perform the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*) with the words beginning "New," and so forth. He also describes the fruit of this with the words beginning "It is accomplished," and so forth. It is *anuttara* (unsurpassed) because its intrinsic nature is untainted great bliss (*anāśrava-mahāsukha*). It is *tattva* (reality) because it has the form of the self-deity and the other deities, which are like an illusion (*māyopama*). It is *śiva* (auspicious), meaning the three excellences (*trikalyāṇa*), because it is the reality that is free from affliction.

"Siddhi" (dngos grub) is said to be luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). "Measuring" (*dpag tshad*) and so forth refers to the statement that at the conclusion of meditating on the union (*yuganaddha*), one should taste the nectar (*amṛta*). "The nine gates" (*sgo dgu*) refers to the teaching on its fruit. "That very virtue" (*dge ba de nyid*) means being free from harm throughout the three times, because it is the authentic reality (*bhūtārtha*).

"Blameless" (*bla med*) means that, like an illusion, it takes the form of the supreme deity for both oneself and others. "Accomplished" (*grub par*) and so forth mean that its nature is the great bliss free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

Therein, he indicates the summarized meaning: **forms** refers to colors such as those of the *indragopa* insect and so forth; **seals** refers to the yoga with the deities; **signs** refers to the skull-cup and so forth; **substances** refers to the five nectars and so forth; **meditations** refers to [the meditations] for activities such as summoning and so forth; **cultivations** refers to the various means in the sequence of clear realizations (*abhisamaya*); **goddesses** refers to the female deities; and **those desired by the mind** refers to [attainments] beginning with the sword and ending with the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).

In order to study the summarized meaning of the tantra, [the passage] beginning with "Form" (*rūpa*) and so forth refers to the colors of the secret organ and so on. "Mudrā" refers to the yoga of the deity. "Signs" (*cihna*) refers to the skull-cup and so forth. "Substances" (*dravya*) refers to the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth. "Meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*) refers to summoning and so forth.

"PAI LAS RNAMS SO" refers to the actions of the *pāda*. "SGOM PA" (Meditation) refers to the stages of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). "Rnam pa sna tshogs thabs" (Various methods) and "lHa mo" (Goddesses) refer to the goddesses themselves. "Yid la 'dod pa" (Mental desires) refers to the sword and so forth, up to the ultimate attainment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). He speaks of the greatness of the tantra with the words beginning "yasya" and so on. This is the self-nature of the book. [015.jpg-upper] = 11v verso
"He maintains" means by placing his hands upon his chest; "to speech" means by looking at the book; "he cultivates" means by means of the sequence of the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*).

Regarding the statement on the greatness of the tantra, the passage beginning with "by whom" and so forth constitutes the nature of the book itself. "Grasping" means to take it into one's possession; "reciting" refers to seeing the book; and "meditating" refers to practicing according to the sequence of the four sessions.

Regarding this, some claim that the Blessed One is not in meditative absorption (*samāpanna*). This is incorrect, because there are indeed words here that directly indicate meditative absorption. As was stated previously: "Always together with wisdom, means, and so forth," and likewise, "having attained such a union. Furthermore, it was said after establishing the state of being the *pañcakulakalāpinī*: "In that way, the accomplishment of yoga (*yogasiddhi*) will come to be."

Yoga, which consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), has been explained. This is because of such statements as, "furthermore, [it is attained] through the application of the two organs," and so forth; thus, one is indeed in a state of meditative union (*samāpanna*). Moreover, enlightenment consisting of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) is what we must achieve. And without being in a state of meditative union, we cannot accomplish the attainment characterized by the nature of supreme bliss. Furthermore, for us, supreme bliss does not consist merely of laughter, gazing, or sexual intercourse, nor is it capable of becoming a defining characteristic [for us]. For what would be manifested by us while remaining therein through the two organs...?

Regarding this, some say that the Blessed One has no meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). The meaning of this is understood as "an incorrect meditative absorption. Here, there is certainly a verse-quarter [that clarifies] what was taught where: "By means of the union of skillful means and wisdom, etc., 'always' means that one should know it to be thus, in that manner, through such union."

Having understood that one must act while possessing the aspects of the five families, it was said; likewise, for the sake of attaining the siddhi of yoga, the yoga consisting of skillful means and wisdom was taught. Furthermore, although the union of the two organs was also seen [in other contexts], it is the actual meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) that I [intend].

If one is able to accomplish the mark [of the Buddha] through the nature of supreme joy—excluding the practice for attaining enlightenment and the meditative absorptions (samāpatti) characterized by the nature of supreme joy—then it is by means of the nature of supreme joy, characterized by passion for smiling and gazing, that I am marked, and not otherwise.

It is not so; for although it is so, I shall abide in that and enter the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the two-fold visualization. By means of the application of the supreme equality of signs, I shall definitively signify [the truth].
This concludes the *Pañjikā* titled *Śrīmahāmāyā*, composed by the great learned master, the venerable Śrī Alaṃkāra.
